unit.title: Diversification
unit.description: Spreading it well: companies, assets, countries, index portfolios, factors and ESG

u29l1.title: Diversifying: the only free thing in finance

texts: All your eggs in one basket
Bruno
I've put my €3,000 into a single company. It's going to be the next big tech giant!
I know it well: I've read everything there is about it.
What do you tell him?
Perfect: if you know it, there's no risk
Knowing it doesn't protect it from fraud, a failed product or bankruptcy.
Spread it out: across lots of companies, one bankruptcy barely shows
That's it! If a company is 0.1 % of your money, its disaster hardly shows.
Buy one more, then you've got two
Better than one, but two companies is still very few.
A single company can fall **90 %**. To recover, you'd need **+900 %**.
Phew. And if I spread it out, is there no risk at all?
There are two kinds of risk. Let's separate them.
One company or all of them?
**Specific** risk hits one particular company. **Market** risk hits them all at once. Which is which?
Specific: one company
Market: all of them
Accounting fraud at a company
It only happens to one: in an index of thousands of companies, it barely shows.
A global recession
It hits almost every company at once: more shares don't dilute it.
A company's flagship product flops
A problem for that company, not for the whole economy.
A pandemic that shuts down the economy
It affects the whole market: spreading across more shares doesn't avoid it.
A long strike at a company's factory
It only slows that company down: its competitors keep selling.
The central bank suddenly raises interest rates
It changes the price of money for every company at once.
Sort the six scares.
Diversifying **removes specific risk**: one bankruptcy weighs little among thousands of companies. **Market risk** doesn't go away with more shares; it's only softened by mixing in bonds or cash.
Ask yourself: does it happen to one company or to the whole economy?
Nicely sorted! Now for the only free lunch.
Sort each scare

steps.title: The free lunch
steps.body:
A single share moves 30-35 % a year; 20-30 shares from different sectors, around 20 %; a global index, 15 %.

Harry Markowitz, Nobel Prize in Economics, called this **the only free lunch**: less risk without giving up expected return.
steps.key: With lots of companies, the disasters of some are offset by the successes of others.
steps.tip: Don't put all your eggs in one basket, or all your baskets on the same lorry.

texts: Shares, bonds and gold since 2008
Real data from 2008 to 2025. You have **€10,000**, all in US shares. Mix them with bonds and gold and look at the worst fall.
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Gold
Between January 2008 and February 2009, shares fell 45 %. What did bonds do?
They fell even further
They gained a little
They fell just as much
US bonds **gained 2 %** while shares lost 45 %. They didn't move together.
Find a mix whose worst fall is half at most (−23 %) and that still gains more than 300 %.

Shares, bonds and gold had their worst runs in different years (2009, 2022 and 2015). Mixing them cuts the worst fall from **−46 %** to around **−20 %**: that's combining assets with **low correlation**.
All in shares: look at the hole in 2008 and 2009.
Half the scare! And look how much you still make.
Lower the shares and split the rest between bonds and gold
Three funds, one portfolio
Marta
I've got three funds: MSCI World, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100. Super diversified, right?
What do you tell her?
Yes: they're three different indices
Three names, almost the same portfolio: the US and big tech show up in all of them.
They overlap a lot: they'll move almost the same
Exactly: their correlation is very high. One global fund would do almost the same job.
You need more funds: ten would be better
More funds buying the same things don't reduce the risk.
OK. So what protects me when everything falls?
In a panic, almost everything risky falls at once: **correlations rise**.
High-quality bonds and cash usually protect you.
But not always: in 2022, shares −18 % and bonds −13 %.

steps.title: How it's measured
steps.body:
**Correlation** tells you whether two assets move together. It ranges from **+1** (always the same way) to **−1** (always the opposite way). **0** means there's no relationship.

• S&P 500 and Euro Stoxx 50: high (0.7-0.9).
• Two big cryptos: very high.
• Shares and high-quality bonds: low or negative in many crises.
• Shares and gold: low and variable.
steps.key: Truly diversifying means owning things that don't all sink on the same day.

texts: Choose your allocation
Real data from 2008 to 2025. You start with **€10,000**, all in bonds. Raise the shares and see how far the portfolio fell at its worst.
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Gold
With everything in shares since 2008, how far did the portfolio fall at its worst?
Almost half
All of it
**46 %** between 2008 and 2009, dividends included. With 60 % in shares and 40 % in bonds, 27 %.
Put at least 60 % in shares without the worst fall going beyond 30 %.
Your **split between shares, bonds and cash** decides how far your portfolio can fall. Here, with the rest in bonds: 40 % in shares, −21 %; 60 %, −27 %; 80 %, −37 %; 100 %, −46 %.
Almost half, gone. Could you hold on without selling?
You're over 30 %: lower the shares a little.
Very calm… but look how little it grows.
More growth, with falls you can still stomach.
Raise the shares little by little
The deposit for the flat
Pablo
I've got €15,000 for the deposit on a flat. I'm buying in 2 years.
It's all in the stock market, because in the long run it goes up.
What do you tell him?
Well done: in the long run it always goes up
In 2 years there's no «long run». A 30 % fall would leave him without a deposit.
Move it to something low-risk, like a fixed-term savings account or a money market fund
That's it! Money you'll need soon shouldn't depend on the stock market.
Leave half in the market, in case it goes up
Less risk, but that half can still fall just before he buys.
What about retirement? I've got 35 years to go.
That's where plenty of shares make sense: there's time to recover from the falls.

steps.title: Example allocations
steps.body:
Classic studies (Brinson and others): this split explains most of how a diversified portfolio swings.

• Conservative: 20-40 % shares (possible fall: −10 to −20 %).
• Moderate: 50-60 % (−20 to −30 %).
• Bold: 70-90 % (−30 to −45 %).
• 100 % shares: −50 % or more.

The closer your goal, the fewer shares. An old rule of thumb is «100 minus your age» in shares; today many people use 110 or 120 minus their age. These are educational examples, not recommendations.
steps.key: A long horizon allows more shares; a short horizon calls for more bonds and cash.

texts: Japan, 1989
It's December 1984 and the Japanese stock market just keeps rising. You invest **€10,000** in its index, the Nikkei. **Real data**, month by month. You can sell whenever you like.
It runs until 2025, whether you sell or not.
In 1989, Japan was the biggest stock market in the world. From its peak it fell **80 %** and took **34 years** to get back there. Betting everything on one country, whichever it is, is concentrating.
You've sold. Look at what comes next…
Almost twenty years later, below what you put in. Are you staying?
You've tripled your money! Who wouldn't want to be here?
Hit Start. You can sell whenever you like
The second risk: currency
You buy **€1,000** worth of shares in a US company. Your result in euros depends on the shares… and on the **dollar**.
dollar
The shares don't move all year, but the dollar falls 10 % against the euro. What happens to you?
Nothing: the shares haven't moved
You lose about 10 %
You gain about 10 %
Your shares are worth the same in dollars, but each dollar gets you fewer euros: **−10 %** without the shares moving.
Find a case where the shares rise and you still lose money in euros.
Outside the euro there's **a second risk: currency**. With long-term shares it's usually accepted; with **bonds**, which move little, people usually pick funds **hedged to euros**.
The dollar is eating your gain.
Shares and dollar both in your favour: double the joy… and double the risk.
Move the shares and the dollar

steps.title: Home bias
steps.body:
We tend to invest in what we know: **home bias**. But Spain is **less than 1 %** of the global stock market, and the US is around 60-70 % of the developed-markets index.

A global index spreads across dozens of countries and currencies: if one region has a bad decade, you don't bear the whole cost.
steps.key: Diversifying across countries reduces the risk of picking «the Japan of the next 30 years».

texts: Just the S&P 500?
Laura
Online, everyone puts everything in the S&P 500. Should I just do that and be done?
What do you tell her?
Yes: the US always rises the most
Not always: in 2000-2009 US shares returned almost nothing while other regions rose.
Better a global index: it already includes the US
That's it! And it covers you if the US has a bad decade, like 2000-2009.
No: the US will never rise again
Nobody knows. It's not about predicting, it's about not depending on one country.
And how many funds do I need to be well diversified?
One can be enough: a global index holds thousands of companies from dozens of countries.
What you need and what you don't
A simple index portfolio has **one, two or three funds**. What does it really need?
Needed
Not needed
Deciding the split between shares and bonds
It's the decision that matters most for how your portfolio moves.
Holding 20 different funds
With one to three index funds you already own thousands of companies.
Low-cost funds
What you don't pay in fees stays invested for you.
Switching every year to the fund that rose most
One year's winners rarely repeat: you turn up late to every trend.
An automatic contribution every month
Consistency does more than timing the market.
Checking the market every day
It only adds stress: reviewing once a year is enough.
Sort the six ideas.
What you do need: **allocation, low costs and consistency**. Not lots of funds, not chasing the year's winner, not checking the market daily.
Does this cut risk or cost, or does it just make work?
Sort each idea

steps.title: One, two or three products
steps.body:
• **One product:** a global fund or ETF (MSCI ACWI or FTSE All-World), with thousands of companies from developed and emerging markets.
• **Two:** global shares + high-quality global bonds hedged to euros.
• **Three:** developed markets (MSCI World) + emerging markets (10-12 %, roughly their global weight) + bonds.

These are examples to understand how they're built, not personalised recommendations.
steps.key: With one to three index funds you can own thousands of companies from all over the world.
steps.tip: A boring portfolio is a portfolio that works.

u29l6.title: Factors: size, value, quality and momentum

texts: Which factor is it?
A **factor** is a trait that, on average and over decades, has been linked to different returns. **Size** is easy: small companies. Sort the other three.
Value
Quality
Momentum
Low P/E and trades below its book value
Cheap compared with what it earns and what it owns: value factor.
Highly profitable and almost debt-free
High profitability and a healthy balance sheet: quality factor.
Up 60 % over the last year
What's risen most in recent months: momentum.
Trades cheaply compared with the profits it makes each year
A low price for what it earns: value.
High margins and steady profits for years
A solid, steady business: quality.
Among the biggest risers of the last six months
Buying what's been rising: momentum.
Sort the six companies.
Size, value, quality and momentum are **portfolio tilts**. Eugene Fama and Kenneth French documented the size and value premiums in the 90s, but they're **averages over decades**, not a guarantee.
Value looks at the price; quality, at the business; momentum, at what's risen.
Sort each company
Pablo's value fund
Pablo
I read that the value factor beat the market over the last century. I put everything into a value fund.
Three years on, I'm 15 % behind the index.
What do you tell him?
Switch to the factor that's done best
Hopping from factor to factor is chasing the past: you buy high and sell low.
It can lag for many years: decide whether you can stick with it
That's it. If you can't, a whole-market index is a better fit.
Take out a loan and buy more, it'll bounce back
With borrowed money, a few bad years can force you to sell at the worst moment.
Value did worse than the market for much of **2007-2020**.
And factor funds («smart beta») usually charge more than an index fund.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: A factor isn't a shortcut: it can spend more than a decade behind the index, and you have to stick with it to collect the premium, if it comes. And once lots of investors know about a factor, its premium can shrink.
steps.key: Factors are a way of tilting your portfolio, not a guarantee of beating the market.

texts: E, S or G?
**ESG** stands for three areas: **environmental**, **social** and **governance**. Which one does each topic belong to?
Environmental (E)
Social (S)
Governance (G)
A factory's CO₂ emissions
Emissions, energy and waste: environmental.
Workplace accidents
Working conditions: social.
Independent board members
Who keeps management in check: governance.
Water and waste management
Impact on the environment: environmental.
Huge bonuses for top management
Executive pay: governance.
Customer data protection
How it treats its customers: social.
Sort the six topics.

ESG measures how a company handles certain **environmental, social and governance risks**. An ESG fund can **exclude** sectors (tobacco, weapons) or pick the best companies in each sector, and it doesn't guarantee higher or lower returns.
E: the planet. S: people. G: who's in charge and how.
Sort each topic
The «Green Future» fund
Marta
Look at this ad: «Green Future». Forests, wind turbines… I'm in!
Although its biggest holdings include oil companies. Weird, right?
What do you tell her?
If it's called green, it must be green
The name and the ad aren't enough: what counts is what's inside.
Check its documents, its SFDR classification and its holdings
Nice! That's how you tell a sustainable fund from a case of **greenwashing**.
Forget sustainable investing: it's all lies
There are serious funds. The problem is not checking.
Not even ESG rating agencies agree.
An MIT study (2022) found an average correlation of only **0.54** between their scores.
The European label
The EU's **SFDR** regulation sorts funds into three articles. Put each fund in its place.
Article 6
Article 8
Article 9
Equity fund with no sustainability goal at all
Article 6: it promises nothing environmental or social.
Fund whose objective is sustainable investment
Article 9: sustainability is its objective.
Fund that promotes environmental characteristics
Article 8: it promotes them, but they aren't its objective.
Classic index fund that doesn't mention sustainability
Article 6: no sustainability goal.
Fund whose objective is to cut emissions measurably
Article 9: its objective is sustainable investment.
Fund that promotes social characteristics, such as good working conditions
Article 8: it promotes them, but doesn't pursue a sustainable objective.
Place the six funds.
Since 2025, ESMA has required any fund with ESG terms in its name to invest **at least 80 %** in assets that meet those characteristics. Read **what's inside**, not just the name.
6: nothing. 8: promotes it. 9: it's the objective.
Place each fund

u29l1-1.prompt: Which risk do you eliminate by spreading your money across hundreds of shares?
u29l1-1.explanation: A bankruptcy stops being a drama if it's 0.1 % of your money. But if the whole market falls, they all fall: that risk is only softened with bonds or cash.

u29l1-2.prompt: You split €10,000 equally across 20 shares. One goes bankrupt and loses all its value; the rest stay the same. How many euros do you lose?
u29l1-2.explanation: 10,000 ÷ 20 = €500 per share. With a single share, that bankruptcy would have wiped out the whole €10,000.

u29l1-4.prompt: Practice exercise (not a recommendation): split €10,000 across these shares. Rules: at least 6 companies, none above 20 % and no sector above 30 %.
u29l1-4.explanation: Spreading across companies and sectors reduces specific risk. Even so, 8 shares is still very few: an index has hundreds or thousands.

u29l1-6.prompt: What is NOT diversifying? Select all that apply.
options: A global share fund and a bond fund
Having almost everything in shares of the company you work for
Owning 10 funds that all buy the same 50 tech companies
u29l1-6.explanation: Different names aren't different assets: cryptos tend to fall together and overlapping funds buy the same things.

u29l1-8.prompt: Pablo has 80 % of his savings in shares of the company he works for: «I know it better than anyone». What do you tell him?
options: That he's concentrating two risks in one place: his salary and his savings
That he should move everything to another company he likes more
He's right: knowing the company eliminates the risk
u29l1-8.explanation: Concentrating in your own employer is a double risk. Diversifying reduces it without giving up expected return.
feedback: That's it: if the company stumbles, it hits him from both sides. It's exactly the risk diversifying eliminates.
Swapping one company for another leaves the same problem: everything in one basket.
Knowing it doesn't protect it from a sector crisis. And if it goes badly, Pablo loses his salary and his savings at the same time.

u29l1-9.prompt: Markowitz called diversification «the only ____ lunch» in finance.
u29l1-9.explanation: You reduce risk without paying for it with lower expected return.

u29l1-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: No: if they all fall at once, it's like owning just one
u29l1-10.explanation: Highly correlated assets don't diversify. And remember: with crypto you can lose everything you put in.
feedback: Well spotted! Diversifying means owning things that behave differently, not lots of names.
If only… but when bitcoin falls hard, most of the others fall with it.
The newest ones tend to be even more volatile. More names doesn't mean less risk.

u29l2-1.prompt: Match each correlation with its meaning.
u29l2-1.explanation: The closer to +1, the less one protects you from the other.
right: They always move in opposite directions
They tend to move in the same direction
They always move the same way

u29l2-2.prompt: Which pair usually has the higher correlation?
u29l2-2.explanation: The big cryptos tend to rise and fall together: combining them barely diversifies at all.

u29l2-3.prompt: This is how gold moved between 2018 and summer 2020, including the stock market crash of March 2020. What trend do you see? (Gold · weekly closes · up to 03/08/2020)
u29l2-3.explanation: While stock markets were sinking, gold went its own way: that's why its correlation with shares is said to be low.

u29l2-4.prompt: January 2022: US Treasury bonds with more than 20 years to maturity. Inflation is soaring and the Federal Reserve announces rate rises. What did they do over the following months?
u29l2-4.explanation: A bond's price depends heavily on interest rates: that's why its relationship with shares changes with inflation.

options: Two funds tracking the MSCI World
u29l2-5.explanation: Developed stock markets and cryptos move closely together; high-quality bonds and gold tend to go their own way more.

u29l2-6.prompt: Marta has three funds: one tracking the MSCI World, another the S&P 500 and another the Nasdaq 100. She says she's very diversified. What do you think?
options: She'd only be diversified with 10 funds
They overlap a lot: they'll move almost the same
She's right: they're three different indices
u29l2-6.explanation: What diversifies is combining assets with low correlation, not adding up similar funds.
feedback: More funds buying the same thing don't reduce risk.
Exactly: their correlation is very high. One global fund would do almost the same with less hassle.
Three names, almost the same portfolio: the US weighs heavily in all three and the big tech companies repeat.

u29l2-10.prompt: In most stock market panics, what has protected a portfolio best?
options: More shares from other developed countries
u29l2-10.explanation: Other countries' stock markets usually fall at the same time. High-quality bonds and cash are what move least with them.

u29l3-1.prompt: Which decision explains most of the swings in a diversified portfolio?
options: Picking the fund that rose most last year
The split between shares, bonds and cash
Which day of the week you buy
u29l3-1.explanation: It's asset allocation: the main lever for the risk you take on.

u29l3-2.prompt: You have €10,000 in a portfolio of 60 % shares and 40 % bonds. Shares fall 40 % and bonds stay the same. How much does your portfolio fall in total?

u29l3-3.prompt: Match each example profile with its typical allocation.
options: Very bold with a long horizon
u29l3-3.explanation: More shares: higher expected return and steeper falls.

u29l3-4.prompt: Ana is 25 and investing for 30 years from now. Example of a bold allocation: put between 70 % and 90 % in shares and at least 10 % in bonds.
options: Global bond fund hedged to euros
u29l3-4.explanation: With 30 years ahead, a share-heavy allocation has time to recover from falls. It's an example for learning, not a recommendation.

u29l3-7.prompt: An old rule of thumb says: put «100 minus your ____» in shares.
u29l3-7.explanation: Today many people use 110 or 120 minus their age. It's only a guideline.

u29l3-8.prompt: Using the «110 minus your age» rule, what percentage in shares would you get at 30?
u29l3-8.explanation: 110 − 30 = 80 % in shares. It's a guideline: your tolerance for falls matters too.

options: Better an allocation with some bonds that you can actually stick with
The best thing is not to invest at all
Your cousin's right: 100 % shares and hold on
u29l3-10.explanation: Your allocation depends on your horizon and also on what you can stomach without selling.
feedback: That's it! The best mix is the one you don't abandon in the next fall.
That way you avoid the falls, but inflation eats away at your savings bit by bit.
By age you could, but you know you sold at −30 %. A plan you can't stick with is no use.
lines: My cousin says at 25 you should be 100 % in shares.
But in 2020 I sold everything when it dropped 30 % 😬

u29l4-1.prompt: Roughly how much does the Spanish stock market weigh in the global stock market?
u29l4-1.explanation: That's why a Spain-only portfolio is very concentrated, even with 35 companies.

u29l4-3.prompt: You own a US share that's worth $100 all year. The euro goes from 1.00 to 1.10 dollars. How many euros is it worth now? (round it)
u29l4-3.explanation: 100 ÷ 1.10 ≈ €90.91: you lose 9 % purely because of the currency, without the share moving.

u29l4-4.prompt: Split a share portfolio by region. Rules: at least 4 funds, none above 60 % and no more than 10 % in Spain.
u29l4-4.explanation: A global index does this split on its own, based on the size of each market. It's an example for practice, not a recommendation.

u29l4-5.prompt: Bruno puts everything in the IBEX 35: «They're the companies I know». What do you tell him?
options: That it's home bias: he's concentrated in less than 1 % of the world
Well done: knowing the companies reduces risk
That he should switch everything to Japan, it's cheaper
u29l4-5.explanation: Investing at home feels safe, but it concentrates. The whole world is the biggest basket.
feedback: That's it. He can keep some Spain, but spreading across the world greatly reduces single-country risk.
Knowing the brands doesn't stop the whole country from having a bad decade.
Moving from one country to another is still concentrating.

u29l4-8.prompt: The tendency to invest mainly in your own country is called ____ bias.
u29l4-8.explanation: It's also called local bias or domestic bias.

u29l4-9.prompt: What are the advantages of spreading across countries? Select all that apply.
options: It reduces dependence on a single country's economy
It gives you access to companies and sectors your country doesn't have
If one region has a bad decade, you don't bear the whole cost
u29l4-9.explanation: It reduces country risk, not market risk: if the world falls, your portfolio falls.

u29l4-10.prompt: Why do people usually choose the euro-hedged version of bond funds?
options: Because the currency could move more than the bonds themselves
u29l4-10.explanation: A high-quality bond may barely move; a 10 % currency swing would wipe out its role as a stabiliser.

u29l5-1.prompt: Match each example portfolio with what it holds.
u29l5-1.explanation: The proportion of shares to bonds depends on your profile and horizon.

u29l5-2.prompt: Roughly how many companies does a global index like the MSCI ACWI or the FTSE All-World hold?
u29l5-2.explanation: From dozens of developed and emerging countries, in a single product.

u29l5-3.prompt: Build an example portfolio with three funds. Rules: use all three, emerging markets between 5 % and 15 %, and bonds between 20 % and 40 %.
options: Global bond fund hedged to euros
u29l5-3.explanation: Emerging markets close to their global weight and bonds according to your profile: that's how a three-fund portfolio is built. Educational example, not a recommendation.

u29l5-4.prompt: Your portfolio is 70 % in a global fund charging 0.20 %, 10 % in emerging markets at 0.25 % and 20 % in bonds at 0.10 %. What's the average annual cost?

u29l5-7.prompt: Every January, Laura switches to the fund that rose most the year before. What's most likely to happen?
options: She ends up buying high what has already risen and paying more in costs
She always has the best fund
u29l5-7.explanation: Past success hardly ever predicts the future. A simple, stable portfolio beats most switching.
feedback: Exactly: chasing the winner usually works out worse than sticking with a cheap index.
One year's winners rarely repeat: she tends to arrive late to every trend.
If she sells to switch (rather than doing a tax-free fund transfer, a Spanish «traspaso»), she may pay more tax, not less.

u29l5-8.prompt: Put the steps for building a simple index portfolio in order.
options: Review and rebalance once a year
Decide the split between shares and bonds
u29l5-8.explanation: First the split (the key decision), then the products and then the discipline.

u29l6-1.prompt: Match each factor with the companies it looks for.
u29l6-1.explanation: These are the four most studied tilts.
right: Those that have risen most in recent months
Cheap relative to earnings or book value

u29l6-2.prompt: A momentum strategy buys whatever has risen most over the last year. What trend do you see in this chart? (Tesla · weekly closes · up to 21/12/2020)
u29l6-2.explanation: A year of very strong gains: exactly what a momentum strategy would look for.

u29l6-3.prompt: December 2020: Tesla has multiplied its price in a year and joins the S&P 500. A momentum strategy would buy it. What did it do over the next two years?
u29l6-3.explanation: A factor premium is an average across thousands of shares over decades; in a single share over a single period, anything can happen.

u29l6-4.prompt: Who documented the size and value premiums in the 90s?
u29l6-4.explanation: Their three-factor model (market, size and value) is the basis of this approach.

u29l6-7.prompt: The strategy that buys whatever has risen most recently is called ____.
u29l6-7.explanation: It relies on trends tending to continue for a while, although they sometimes reverse suddenly.

u29l6-10.prompt: What are the limits of factors? Select all that apply.
options: Their funds tend to be more expensive
When lots of people know about them, the premium can shrink
They can lag the index for years
u29l6-10.explanation: Nothing guarantees beating the market: factors are a reasonable bet, not a certainty.

u29l7-1.prompt: Match each letter with what it measures.

u29l7-2.prompt: Under the EU's SFDR regulation, which funds have sustainable investment as their objective?
u29l7-2.explanation: Article 8 funds only «promote» environmental or social characteristics.

u29l7-6.prompt: What can be signs of greenwashing? Select all that apply.
options: It publishes its selection method and exclusions
Vague promises like «investing in a better planet» with no data
Heavy polluters among its largest holdings with no explanation why
Lots of green marketing and little concrete information
u29l7-6.explanation: Transparency (method, exclusions, holdings) is the opposite of greenwashing.

u29l7-8.prompt: Presenting something as sustainable when it isn't really is called ____.
u29l7-8.explanation: That's why ESMA now requires funds with ESG terms in their names to meet certain minimums.

u29l7-9.prompt: What does an «exclusion» ESG fund do?
options: Leaves out entire sectors, such as tobacco or weapons
u29l7-9.explanation: Another approach is «best in class»: picking the best companies in each sector.

u29l7-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: ESG is just marketing, forget it
Look at its SFDR classification, exclusions, holdings and cost
u29l7-10.explanation: ESG can reflect your values, but it means reading the small print.
feedback: If only. That's where greenwashing comes in: you have to look inside.
There's a bit of everything. With information you can choose wisely.
Perfect! And compare it with a regular index fund: cost matters too.
lines: I want my money to support responsible companies 🌱
Is it enough for the fund to have ESG in its name?
